content: Valganciclovir is an antiviral medication that is converted in the body to its active form, ganciclovir. It is primarily used to prevent cytomegalovirus (CMV) disease in individuals who have undergone organ transplants. CMV disease can cause severe infections in the body, including CMV retinitis, an eye infection that may lead to blindness. Valganciclovir works by slowing the growth of the CMV virus. It is also used to treat CMV retinitis in individuals with advanced HIV disease (AIDS). However, it is important to note that valganciclovir is not a cure for CMV disease, and some individuals may experience worsening of CMV retinitis despite treatment. Before starting valganciclovir, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, ganciclovir, acyclovir, or any other substances. This medication may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Valganciclovir can cause dizziness or drowsiness, which may be worsened by alcohol or marijuana (cannabis). Limit alcohol consumption while taking this medication. Valganciclovir can increase your susceptibility to infections or worsen existing infections. Avoid contact with individuals who have contagious illnesses, such as chickenpox, COVID-19, measles, or the flu. Inform your healthcare provider that you are taking valganciclovir before receiving any vaccinations or immunizations. During pregnancy, valganciclovir should only be used when absolutely necessary, as it may harm an unborn baby. Discuss the potential risks and benefits with your doctor. Women of childbearing age should undergo a pregnancy test before starting this medication. To prevent pregnancy, men with female partners should use effective barrier protection, such as latex or polyurethane condoms, during treatment and for at least 90 days after stopping the medication. Women of childbearing age should use reliable forms of birth control, such as birth control pills and condoms, during treatment and for at least 30 days after stopping the medication. It is unknown if valganciclovir passes into breast milk, but due to potential risks to the infant, breastfeeding is not recommended while using this medication. Valganciclovir may interact with other medications, potentially altering their effects or increasing the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal supplements, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Some medications, such as cancer chemotherapy, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, zidovudine, or cyclosporine, may decrease bone marrow function, lower blood cell counts, or cause kidney problems. Valganciclovir is very similar to ganciclovir, so do not take ganciclovir in place of valganciclovir without consulting your doctor or pharmacist. If someone overdoses on valganciclovir and experiences severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. While taking valganciclovir, your doctor will monitor your health through regular blood tests, kidney function tests, and eye exams. Keep all medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store valganciclovir tablets at room temperature, away from light and moisture. The liquid form of this medication should be stored in the refrigerator but not frozen. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Valganciclovir can cause side effects such as diarrhea, upset stomach, dizziness, drowsiness, unsteadiness, or shaking (tremors). Remember that your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. If you experience any unusual or severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately. For medical advice about side effects in the U.S., call your doctor. In Canada, consult your doctor for guidance. Valganciclovir may reduce bone marrow function, leading to a decrease in red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. This can result in anemia, a weakened immune system, and bleeding problems. Your doctor will monitor your blood test results and adjust your treatment to minimize these risks. Additionally, valganciclovir may reduce fertility in both men and women and has been shown to cause tumors in laboratory animals. Although there is no conclusive evidence in humans, valganciclovir should be considered potentially carcinogenic. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
